1.pericope_label: Wisdom hath builded her house, she hath hewn out her seven pillars... she hath killed her beasts; she hath mingled her wine; she hath also furnished her table

schools.summary: Delitzsch and Ellicott both read the building and the feast as deliberate allegory rather than narrative, but part company over how far the detail may be pressed: Delitzsch confines the seven pillars to the self-communicating virtues of Wisdom's own nature and refuses to allegorize the menu, while Ellicott identifies the house with Christ's incarnate flesh and with the church.
Gill reads the house christologically as the human nature of Christ, a temple built without the hands of men, and the slain beasts as the sacrifice of the cross, vicarious and never to be repeated.

Clarke rejects the sacramental allegory outright and takes the house for the universe framed by the eternal counsel of God, the provision being God's ample supply for all creatures; Wesley takes seven for many and the pillars for prophets, apostles and ministers.
Henry hears the Word of God speaking and takes the house for heaven and the church at once, pressing that the word for the slaughter is sacrifice, so that this is a feast upon a sacrifice.

debates.question: What is the house with seven pillars?

positions.view: The incarnate nature of Christ, or the church built upon it.
The created universe, framed on the plan set out in the previous chapter.
The seven virtues of Wisdom's own nature communicating themselves, with no further identification attempted.

debates.question: Are the slain beasts a sacrifice?

positions.view: Yes; the term is sacrifice, and the feast is a feast upon it.
No; the noun used is the ordinary word for slaughter outside the sacrificial system, and the beast is simply an ox.
The provision is God's supply for the creatures that people created nature.

outliers.note: Dismisses the patristic and sacramental readings of the pillars, beasts and wine as strange creatures of the interpreters' own brain.
Argues from the tense of the verbs that this is not a parable at all but an allegorical picture of a present reality.

themes: Wisdom hath builded her house, she hath hewn out her seven pillars:
She hath killed her beasts; she hath mingled her wine; she hath also furnished her table.

3.pericope_label: She hath sent forth her maidens: she crieth upon the highest places of the city... Forsake the foolish, and live; and go in the way of understanding

schools.summary: Delitzsch tracks the point at which the allegory breaks down, the maidens receding and Wisdom speaking in her own person, and reads the closing summons as addressed to the simple themselves; Ellicott notes that the parallel parable sends servants rather than maidens and takes the same summons as a call to stop being weak.

Gill identifies the maidens as ministers of the Gospel, guards the figure against any inference about women's preaching, and reads the bread as the whole provision of Christ's house, chiefly Christ himself.

Clarke turns the invitation into a charge to study creation to its fountain head and holds that the mingled wine was strengthened with spices rather than diluted; Wesley says flatly that it was mingled with water, as the custom of hot countries was.

debates.question: What does it mean to forsake the foolish?

positions.view: Abandon the company of foolish men, and foolish things with them.
The simple are themselves addressed and told to leave off their simplicity, since it would be a strange thing for the simple to forsake the simple.
Wine diluted with water, as was customary.
Wine strengthened and flavoured with spices rather than weakened.
Spiced to improve the flavour, though the Passover cup was watered to decrease its strength.

outliers.note: Reports a surviving Asiatic custom of sending invitations to guests' doors by a company of women, offering it as the background of the maidens.
Interrupts the exposition to deny that the maidens sanction women's preaching, holding that the term serves only the decency of the parable.

themes: She hath sent forth her maidens: she crieth upon the highest places of the city,
Whoso is simple, let him turn in hither: as for him that wanteth understanding, she saith to him,
Come, eat of my bread, and drink of the wine which I have mingled.
Forsake the foolish, and live; and go in the way of understanding.

7.pericope_label: He that reproveth a scorner getteth to himself shame... but if thou scornest, thou alone shalt bear it

schools.summary: Delitzsch insists the scorner and the simple are two sharply distinguished classes and reads the wise man's teachableness as a moral rather than intellectual quality; both he and Ellicott take the plural 'holy' as naming the Holy One.
Gill treats the prohibition as the limit of the Gospel invitation, applying it to the Jews who refused the feast and to the Pharisees whom Christ told his disciples to let alone.

Clarke refuses to let the saying license silence, holding that we must not suffer sin upon our neighbour and that reproof is to be given in love until men blaspheme; Wesley reads the verse as identifying the foolish company of the previous verse.

debates.question: What is the knowledge of the holy?

positions.view: Knowledge of the Holy One, the plural being one of majesty.
Knowledge of the holy ones or saints, as the older versions render it.

debates.question: How far does the prohibition on reproving a scorner extend?

positions.view: It withdraws the invitation from whole classes who have mocked at it.
It is prudential only; the duty of faithful reproof stands until men contradict and blaspheme.
It presupposes that scorner and simple are different men, and cannot be made a general rule about company.

outliers.note: Records a long addition to this passage in the Greek, Syriac and Latin, about the man who trusts in falsity and feeds on the winds, absent from the Hebrew.
Reads the promise of lengthened days as concealing its agent, so that the heavenly Powers rather than Wisdom grant the years.

themes: He that reproveth a scorner getteth to himself shame: and he that rebuketh a wicked man getteth himself a blot.
Reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee: rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee.
Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser: teach a just man, and he will increase in learning.
The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.
For by me thy days shall be multiplied, and the years of thy life shall be increased.
If thou be wise, thou shalt be wise for thyself: but if thou scornest, thou alone shalt bear it.

13.pericope_label: A foolish woman is clamorous: she is simple, and knoweth nothing... But he knoweth not that the dead are there; and that her guests are in the depths of hell

schools.summary: Delitzsch explains Folly as the personification the contrast demanded and reads the closing shades as the worn-out who are alive only in appearance, in the depths of Hades; Ellicott presses the imitation, Folly borrowing Wisdom's own words as Satan borrows the form of an angel of light.
Gill identifies Folly with antichrist and the great whore, reading her chapels, her boasted infallibility and her priests as the substance of the passage.

Clarke keeps to the general case, setting Folly's school next door to Wisdom's, and reports the older versions that make the shades the giants of the old world; Wesley grounds the sweetness in the difficulty of obtaining what is forbidden.
Henry takes Folly for carnal sensual pleasure and traces her method in detail, the throne-like seat, the pretence of fashion, and the charge of simplicity levelled at the virtuously educated young.

positions.view: Carnal sensual pleasure personified.
Antichrist, the great whore, and the church of Rome.
Folly as the abstract counterpart the picture required, without further identification.

debates.question: Who are the dead in her house?

positions.view: The shades, the worn-out who only appear to live.
The giants of the old world, as the older versions render the word.
Those who live in pleasure and are dead while they live, already in the depths of hell.

outliers.note: Sustains an anti-Roman reading throughout the section, taking the chapels, the proselytizing and the priests as the literal subject of the passage.
Treats the contemporary stage as a close exposition of the passage, the sober young man being made the fool of the play.

themes: A foolish woman is clamorous: she is simple, and knoweth nothing.
For she sitteth at the door of her house, on a seat in the high places of the city,
To call passengers who go right on their ways:
Whoso is simple, let him turn in hither: and as for him that wanteth understanding, she saith to him,
Stolen waters are sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant.
But he knoweth not that the dead are there; and that her guests are in the depths of hell.
